questions.question: An agent looks both ways, crosses, and is struck by falling cargo. The agent was:

options.A: Neither, because rationality does not apply to physical agents
options.B: Irrational, because it failed to look up
options.C: Irrational, because the outcome was bad
options.D: Rational, because the action maximised expected performance given available information

The chief advantage of a utility function over a goal is that it:

questions.question: Write a full PEAS specification for a system that recommends which barangays should receive relief goods first after a typhoon. Then state one way your performance measure could be gamed, and repair it.
questions.modelAnswer: Answers vary. Specify performance measures over desired environment states, the post-typhoon environment, recommendation or referral actuators, and available sensors. Identify a shortcut that satisfies the initial measure without distributing relief well, then rewrite the measure to reward the intended state of the world.
rubric: Includes Performance measure, Environment, Actuators and Sensors.
questions.source: Module 2, Check your understanding, Part B, question 1
questions.hint2: Define success over barangay outcomes, then block one shortcut.

questions.question: Explain, with an example, the difference between an agent function and an agent programme. Why can the agent function usually not be written down?
questions.modelAnswer: The agent function is the abstract mapping from every finite percept sequence to an action. The agent programme is the finite implementation that approximates that function and runs on an architecture. The function usually cannot be written down because it is a potentially infinite object covering every possible percept history.
rubric: Explains the potentially infinite percept histories.
questions.source: Module 2, Check your understanding, Part B, question 2
questions.hint2: Function: P* → A; programme: the running finite artefact.

questions.question: Classify a ride-hailing dispatch system along all six environment dimensions. For the two hardest dimensions, state what design consequence follows.
questions.modelAnswer: Answers must justify observability, agency, determinism, episodicity, dynamism and continuity for ride-hailing dispatch. Select the two hardest dimensions and connect them to handout consequences such as internal state for partial observability, probability distributions for stochastic outcomes, lookahead for sequential decisions, real-time constraints for dynamism, or optimisation/discretisation for continuity.
rubric: States the corresponding design consequences from the handout.
questions.source: Module 2, Check your understanding, Part B, question 3
questions.hint2: Partial → internal state; stochastic → probabilities; sequential → lookahead; dynamic → real time; continuous → optimisation.

questions.question: A team proposes a simple reflex agent for a system that must decide whether a laboratory workstation has been left logged in. Explain why this architecture fails, and what minimum change fixes it.
questions.modelAnswer: A simple reflex agent uses only the current percept and has no memory, so it cannot track relevant information hidden by partial observability and may repeat identical actions. The minimum fix is a model-based reflex architecture with internal state and a model that tracks how the world evolves and how actions affect it.
rubric: Explains the lack of memory or internal state.
Connects the failure to partial observability.
Selects a model-based reflex agent as the minimum fix.
Explains what internal state or the model contributes.
questions.source: Module 2, Check your understanding, Part B, question 4
questions.hint2: Minimum fix: model-based reflex with internal state.
